maml:description.maml:para: Signs in to Azure - in the browser (OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow with PKCE and a loopback redirect), with a device code, as a service principal (client secret or certificate) or with a managed identity - no Az or Microsoft.Graph module, and no app registration required by default.

Without a sign-in option, the browser (below). -DeviceCode shows a code to enter at https://microsoft.com/devicelogin on any device. -ClientSecret, -CertificatePath and -CertificateThumbprint sign in as a service principal (-ClientId, -TenantId), and -Identity with the managed identity of where this runs (Azure Automation, a VM, App Service): no user, no refresh token - a new token is asked for when one runs out.
The browser sign-in: Opens your default browser to Microsoft's sign-in page, receives the redirect on a one-shot local HTTP listener (http://localhost:<port>/), and exchanges the resulting authorization code for tokens directly against the v2.0 token endpoint over REST - using a PKCE code_verifier / code_challenge pair (RFC 7636) instead of a client secret, which is what makes this safe for a public desktop tool with no back-end to keep a secret in.
By default this uses Azure's well-known public client ID for the Azure CLI (04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46), which is pre-consented in every Entra ID tenant, so sign-in works immediately with no app registration of your own. Pass -ClientId to use your own App Registration instead (create it with the "Mobile and desktop applications" platform and a http://localhost redirect URI).
The resulting session (access token, refresh token, expiry, signed-in account and tenant) is kept in this module's memory for the rest of the PowerShell session and used automatically by every command, such as Invoke-AACPSRule. It is not written to disk.
The .pfx file's password.

maml:description.maml:para: Creates or updates a storage account - and its containers, file shares, queues, tables, blobs and settings - idempotently, with the Azure REST APIs: plan, gates (Azure Policy and PSRule), then apply. No ARM, Bicep or Terraform template.

Works like a Bicep or Terraform deployment, without a template: 1. Desired state your configuration, with the Azure Verified Module's parameter names and its defaults (avm/res/storage/storage-account): StorageV2, Standard_GRS, Hot, TLS 1.2, HTTPS only, no public blob access, infrastructure encryption, network rules denying by default with the AzureServices bypass, blob and container soft delete - enforced on every run, as Bicep would. 2. Plan what exists is read (GET) and compared property by property: Create, Update, No change - or Replace, when Azure can't change a property in place (location, kind, hierarchical namespace, infrastructure encryption...). Containers, shares, queues and tables that exist but aren't configured are Drift (left alone) - or deleted with -Prune. 3. Gates the name (checkNameAvailability); the policy assignments that apply to storage in the resource group; Azure Policy's verdict on the exact body of every write (checkPolicyRestrictions): Deny blocks, Audit is reported, Modify and Append changes are shown; PSRule for Azure - and the module's naming and tag rules - on the account as it will be (shift left): what breaks your standards. 4. Decide blocked stops here, before anything is written: a name taken, an immutable change, a policy Deny, a PSRule rule that fails (or PSRule not running), -FailOn. Each failing PSRule rule comes with its fix - the setting and value, or what to do - and a configuration snippet with all of them; -UseSuggestedFix deploys with those settings (and checks every gate again). A rule that doesn't apply is excluded on purpose with -ExcludeRule. Otherwise you are asked before anything is written (-Force, or -Confirm:$false, for pipelines); -WhatIf stops after the plan. 5. Apply in dependency order, PUT to create, PATCH with only what changed to update (long-running operations followed); role assignments named from scope, principal and role, so they are found again; blobs uploaded only when their MD5 differs. Not a transaction: the first failure stops, and running again carries on. 6. Verify everything read and compared again: the plan must now be "no changes". What Azure changed by itself (a Modify policy) is reported. Running the same configuration again plans no changes and writes nothing.
The configuration: -ConfigurationPath (.psd1, or .json - including an AVM parameters file), and/or parameters, which win over the file: -Name, -Location, -SkuName, -Kind, -AccessTier, -Tag, -Container, -FileShare, -Queue, -Table, -Blob, and -Setting for any other AVM parameter. Supported AVM parameters: name, location, kind, skuName, accessTier, tags, allowBlobPublicAccess, allowSharedKeyAccess, allowCrossTenantReplication, defaultToOAuthAuthentication, minimumTlsVersion, supportsHttpsTrafficOnly, publicNetworkAccess, networkAcls, requireInfrastructureEncryption, largeFileSharesState, enableHierarchicalNamespace, enableNfsV3, enableSftp, isLocalUserEnabled, allowedCopyScope, dnsEndpointType, blobServices (with containers, their roleAssignments, and diagnosticSettings), fileServices (shares), queueServices (queues), tableServices (tables), managementPolicyRules, privateEndpoints (with a private DNS zone group), diagnosticSettings, roleAssignments, lock - and blobs (files to upload: @{ container; path; name; contentType }). maml:description.maml:para: Draws your existing Azure resources as an editable draw.io diagram - resources, the network topology or Application Gateways - with real containers, Azure icons and attached connections; -Update refreshes it from Azure and keeps the changes you made.

Reads Azure (read-only, Reader is enough) the way the map commands do and writes a .drawio file you open and edit in draw.io - the desktop app, app.diagrams.net, the Draw.io Integration for VS Code, Confluence - and export from there to Visio (.vsdx), PNG, SVG or PDF.
-View chooses what is drawn: Resources the resources in resource groups or subscriptions, in subscription > resource group > virtual network > subnet boxes, with their connections: network links, peerings, private endpoints, routes, DNS links and dependencies (as Show-AACResourceMap) Network the network topology of a tenant, management groups, subscriptions or regions: hubs and spokes, peerings, gateways, firewalls and appliances (as Show-AACNetworkTopology) ApplicationGateway each gateway's flow - listeners > rules > backend settings > pools and targets - with probes, WAF policies and health (as Show-AACApplicationGatewayMap) Governance the management group hierarchy: the tenant root and management groups as nested boxes, each subscription inside its group, with the policy and role assignments at each level (as Show-AACManagementGroupMap)
In the diagram: - boxes are draw.io containers: move a box and what is in it moves with it; drag a resource into another box and it belongs there - resources carry the Azure icons (vector), their name and type; unattached ones are red, those outside the selection faded - connections are attached at both ends and follow what you move - each shape keeps its resource ID, type, location, resource group and subscription (Edit > Edit Data, or hover), and Ctrl+click opens it in the Azure portal - a Legend page shows the kinds of box and connection, what was read and when (-NoLegend leaves it out) -SplitBy puts each subscription, resource group, management group, region or gateway on a page of its own, for large estates.

maml:description.maml:para: Exports existing Azure resources as Terraform - a folder ready for terraform init and plan, with the import blocks - through the Azure Export for Terraform API, and shows what couldn't be exported.

Asks Azure to write the Terraform configuration of what you choose - a resource group, resources by ID (or piped from any command that returns resources), or a Resource Graph query - and waits for it.
The export is a long-running operation that Azure does on its side, and its time grows with the number of resources. So the command: - counts the resources first (Resource Graph), and says when an export is large and how to make it faster - with -BatchSize, splits it into exports of that many resources that run at the same time (-ThrottleLimit at once), and merges them into one folder - shows each export as it runs: its status, how long it has run, and how many batches are done - not a percentage Azure doesn't give - saves the operations in export.json as soon as Azure accepts them: after Ctrl+C or -TimeoutMinutes, -Resume collects the result without exporting again
The folder (-Path) gets: terraform.tf the providers the configuration needs providers.tf the provider blocks, with the subscription ID main.tf the resources azapi.tf with -FallbackToAzApi: what azurerm couldn't export, as azapi resources import.tf import blocks, so terraform plan brings the existing resources under Terraform - no terraform import commands to run export.json what was asked, the operations, what was skipped and why Several subscriptions get a folder each, under -Path, exported at the same time.
Several resource groups of one subscription are exported together, in one query (with their child resources), so they share one folder and their names can't clash. With -BatchSize, each batch gets names of its own (res-b1-0, res-b2-0...); a resource two batches both return is kept once. Resources in different batches refer to each other by Azure ID rather than by Terraform address.
What couldn't be exported is listed, never silently dropped: a resource type the azurerm provider doesn't support yet is Skipped - -FallbackToAzApi exports those again with the azapi provider, which covers every Azure resource type. Sensitive values are masked unless -IncludeSensitive.
-Plan proves the export: it runs terraform init, validate and plan in each folder and reads the plan (as Get-AACTerraformPlan does). A faithful export plans only imports; anything else - an attribute Terraform would change - is what the export didn't capture. It needs the terraform CLI, signed in its own way (az login, or ARM_CLIENT_ID, ARM_CLIENT_SECRET and ARM_TENANT_ID): Terraform doesn't use the Connect-AAC sign-in.
The export reads Azure; it changes nothing there. It needs Reader on what is exported, and the Microsoft.AzureTerraform resource provider registered on the subscription - -RegisterProvider registers it (that is a change, so it asks first and honours -WhatIf; registering needs a role such as Contributor).
The API is in preview (api-version 2026-09-01-preview); -ApiVersion picks another.

maml:description.maml:para: Gets every Azure Firewall Policy rule - DNAT, network and application: a colour-coded Spectre.Console view at the prompt, PowerShell objects down a pipeline, and optional CSV, PDF and interactive HTML exports.

Reads the rules of every Azure Firewall Policy the signed-in account can see (or only those in -SubscriptionId / -FirewallPolicyName) from Azure Resource Graph, over REST with the Connect-AAC sign-in - no Az modules needed. One object is returned per rule, sorted as the Azure portal lists them: by policy, rule collection group priority, rule collection priority, then the rule's position in its collection. (Azure Firewall itself applies all DNAT rules first, then network, then application rules, each in that priority order, and a base policy's rules before the policy's own.)
IP Groups used as a source or destination are resolved to their names and addresses, wherever in the tenant they live (one Resource Graph query, no per-group calls). Each rule also carries its policy's base (parent) policy and the firewalls the policy is attached to.

PowerShell can't tell "$r = Get-AACFirewallRule" from a plain call, so to keep the objects in a variable add -PassThru or -NoDisplay.

Read-only, through the Azure DevOps REST API - nothing is changed. For each organization (-Organization, or -DiscoverOrganization) and project (or -Project), it reads: pipelines every build pipeline: YAML or classic (designer, no YAML file), its folder, repository, state and last run, and every classic release pipeline steps YAML pipelines' files from their default branch (Azure Repos Git) and the templates they include - local or template@repository, nested to -TemplateDepth; the script files, package.json scripts and Makefile targets they run (from the pipeline's repository); classic pipelines' tasks, named through the organization's task catalogue repositories the last push, the branch policies on the default branch, GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps (on or off, and active alerts by type and severity) security service connections, variable groups and environments: who may use them, their checks runs the runs of the last -MetricDays and each environment's deployments
Tools: one catalogue (about 150 tools) is matched against every file a pipeline runs - its YAML and templates, script files, package.json scripts, Makefile targets, a classic pipeline's tasks - and against container images (fluxcd/flux-cli...). Categories: Lint, Build, Test, Security, Deploy, Publish, GitOps (Flux, Argo CD, Kustomize...) and Tooling (az, git, jq...). Every match is evidence (-View Evidence): the pipeline, the tool, its version (an installer task, an image tag), how it was found, the file and line, and the line itself (credentials masked). -View Tool is the matrix of tools with their pipelines, projects and versions; -View Coverage which stages each pipeline has; -View Unrecognised the commands scripts run that no rule knows (most-run first) and the templates and files that couldn't be read. -ToolRule and -ToolRulePath add tools of your own.
Tasks (-View Task): every task with its major version and what it does (the task catalogue's description), packages installed at a version, shells, container images, agent images and pools.
Findings: classic pipelines; never run, not run in -StaleDays, last run failed, disabled; no security scanning, no tests, no linting; deprecated or older task versions; unpinned container images; retired hosted images; a value that looks like a secret written in the YAML (its key and line - never the value); unreliable pipelines and long queues; service connections open to every pipeline, using a client secret rather than workload identity federation, or unused; variable groups with secrets outside Key Vault, secret-looking values not marked secret, open to every pipeline; production environments with no approval, environments with no checks or open to every pipeline; default branches with no required reviewers or build validation; Advanced Security off, exposed secrets, critical and high alerts; idle repositories.
SBOM (software bill of materials): which build pipelines generate one - the Microsoft SBOM Tool (sbom-tool generate, the Manifest Generator task, GenerateSBOM=true in .NET projects), 1ES Pipeline Templates, Syft, CycloneDX, Trivy or Docker - and which validate one (sbom-tool validate); then, from each one's latest successful run, the SBOM it published (the _manifest/spdx_2.2 or spdx_3.0 manifest.spdx.json, or any SPDX or CycloneDX JSON file in its artifacts): format, the tool that made it, components and files, completeness against the NTIA minimum elements (name, version, supplier, package URL), licences by kind (permissive, weak or strong copyleft, unknown), and every component with its version, ecosystem, supplier and licence. Branching: every branch with its role (from its name - develop, release/*, hotfix/*, feature/*...), last commit, ahead and behind the default branch, stale after -StaleBranchDays, and the policies on it; each repository's strategy (GitFlow, trunk-based with release branches, trunk-based / GitHub flow, feature branching, single branch). maml:description.maml:para: Assesses Azure Policy across a tenant, management group or set of subscriptions - what is assigned, how compliant it is (overall, by subscription, assignment, policy and category), the exemptions and the managed identities' roles - and what to improve, with a Spectre.Console view, objects, and CSV, PDF and interactive HTML reports. In the spirit of AzPolicyLens (github.com/Azure/AzPolicyLens).

Read-only (Reader is enough), Azure Resource Graph only - no Az modules. Every assignment, exemption, custom definition and initiative, and the management group hierarchy are read tenant-wide, so what a management group assigns to a subscription is there; the built-in definitions that are assigned are read by ID; compliance is read in the subscriptions in scope.
Compliance is counted as AzPolicyLens counts it: each resource once, at its worst state (NonCompliant, then Compliant, Conflict, Exempt), and compliance = (compliant + exempt) / all - overall, by subscription, by management group, by assignment (and subscription), by policy and by category. Under -ComplianceWarningPercent (80) is Warning, under half of it Poor.
Every assigned initiative is opened up (InitiativePolicies, and the initiative-policies CSV and HTML table): each member policy with its effect - an effect override on the assignment included - the value each of its parameters ends up with (from the assignment, else the initiative or the policy's default, as noted) and its compliance. For one row per policy and parameter, see Get-AACAssignedPolicy -ExpandPolicySet.

maml:description.maml:para: Assesses an Azure tenant end to end - the organization, an inventory of every resource type with its key settings and policy compliance, Azure Policy, the Well-Architected Framework, PSRule for Azure, Advisor, retirements, Defender for Cloud, FinOps and cost, outages and quotas - as CSV files, an interactive HTML report, a PDF and interactive diagrams, with a live Spectre.Console progress display.

The module's take on Azure Resource Inventory (ARI), and the one command to run first in a tenant you need to understand: it reads the tenant (or the subscriptions, management groups, resource groups or tag you name) and writes the reports you choose. Read-only; Reader is enough (Security Reader for Defender, Cost Management Reader for cost); no Az modules, no Excel. -Full turns on everything that is off by default.
The focused assessments go deeper into one service or discipline - Invoke-AACWafAssessment (a workload's review, with the team's answers and the trend), Invoke-AACPolicyAssessment, Invoke-AACDefenderAssessment, Invoke-AACGovernanceAssessment and the service ones (AKS, Cosmos DB, Function Apps, Log Analytics, Service Bus, storage, virtual networks).
What it reads, in phases - each a line of the progress display: 1. Scope the subscriptions (with their management groups) in scope, and the tenant's management groups 2. Estate every resource and resource group, the resource types present; Advisor recommendations (and retirements, always); Defender for Cloud (-SecurityCenter); Azure Policy compliance - by policy, resource group and resource (unless -SkipPolicy); support tickets 3. Inventory a sheet per resource type present - ~95 types, in the categories Compute, Hybrid, Containers, Databases, Analytics, AI, Integration, IoT, Management, Monitoring, Networking, Security, Storage and Web - each with the settings that matter for it (a VM's size, power state, OS, disks, IP, network and security settings; a storage account's TLS, public access, shared keys and firewall; ...), as Resource Graph projections 4. Azure APIs per subscription: the Advisor score, reservation recommendations, the budgets, the last 6 months' outages (Resource Health service issues), compute quotas (-QuotaUsage), and VM sizes' vCPUs and memory (unless -SkipVMDetail); -SkipApi skips them all 5. Well-Architected the checks of Invoke-AACWafAssessment across the five pillars - Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence, Performance Efficiency - scored by pillar, design principle and check (unless -SkipWaf) 6. Cost each resource's cost, this month and last (-IncludeCost, Cost Management) 7. PSRule PSRule for Azure's rules on the resources (-PSRule) 8. Governance the policy assignments in force and every policy they apply (unless -SkipPolicy), FinOps, and one list of recommendations 9. Reports the reports asked for (-HtmlPath, -PdfPath, -CsvPath, -DiagramPath), then an upload to a blob container (-StorageAccount)
Every inventory sheet (and All resources) adds, after its own columns: Retirement (an Advisor retirement notice for the resource), Advisor (its number of recommendations), its policy compliance (Policy - Non-compliant, Compliant, Exempt or Not evaluated; Non-compliant policies; Failing policies, by name), WAF gaps (the Well-Architected checks it fails), PSRule failures (with -PSRule), its cost with -IncludeCost, and its tags with -IncludeTag. The overview sheets: Subscriptions, Resource groups, Resource types, All resources; then Advisor recommendations, Advisor score, Retirements, Security recommendations, Secure score, Policy compliance, Outages, Quotas, Support tickets and Reservation recommendations. Then: Well-Architected WAF pillars (score and maturity), WAF design principles, WAF checks and WAF findings (each failed check on each resource, with what to do) FinOps Savings opportunities (by lever: Waste - unattached disks, unused public IPs, VMs stopped but billed, empty plans, old snapshots; Rightsizing and Rate - Advisor's cost recommendations, reservations, savings plans; Licensing - Azure Hybrid Benefit; Modernise - old VM generations - each with its estimated annual saving), Cost allocation (the resources with a cost-allocation tag, -CostTag, and the cost of those without), Budgets (spent and forecast against each budget, the alerts, the subscriptions with none) and, with -IncludeCost, Cost by service, Cost by resource group and Top cost resources (this month projected against last month) and the governance sheets: Policy compliance Compliance by initiative, by resource group and by standard (the controls of CIS, NIST, ISO 27001, the Microsoft cloud security benchmark ... initiatives), and each non-compliant resource with why and how to fix it Policy inventory Policy assignments, and every policy in force with its effect, resource types, controls and status (Failed, Passed, Manual review, Exempt, Not evaluated, Disabled) PSRule results PSRule rules (checked, passed, failed, with their documentation) and the failed resources (-PSRule) Recommendations Resource recommendations: Advisor, Defender, retirements, unattached and empty resources, policy non-compliance, PSRule, the Well-Architected findings and FinOps (budgets, cost allocation) in one list, each with a severity, category and what to do
The reports - each written only where its own parameter says, none by default: -HtmlPath a tabbed workbook: an Executive summary (tiles - the Well-Architected score, the estimated savings, cost-tag coverage ... - charts - a click filters the table behind them - and the tenant tree), then Policy compliance, Policy inventory, Well-Architected, PSRule results, Resource recommendations, FinOps, Resources, Inventory, Advisor, Security and Health; every table searchable, filterable, groupable, with each row's details a click away, and downloadable as CSV -PdfPath the summary, then each category with its sheets' key columns (bookmarked) -CsvPath a folder: a CSV file per sheet -DiagramPath a folder: TenantAssessment-Network.html, the network topology - virtual networks, subnets, peerings, gateways, firewalls, load balancers, private endpoints, NSGs and routes (-DiagramFullEnvironment: every resource and how they connect); TenantAssessment-Organization.html, management groups > subscriptions > resource groups; TenantAssessment-Resources.html, each subscription with its resource types and counts. Interactive: pan, zoom, search, details on click, PNG and SVG export. Without any of them the run shows its summary and returns the assessment (-PassThru, -NoDisplay): every sheet is in its Sheets.

maml:description.maml:para: Assesses the estate against the Azure Well-Architected Framework's five pillars - Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence and Performance Efficiency - scored by pillar, design principle and check, with workbook-style heat maps by subscription, resource group or resource type, findings and what to do, a Spectre.Console view, objects, and CSV, PDF and interactive HTML reports.

Read-only, with one batch of Azure Resource Graph queries - Reader is enough, no Az modules. Every check is evaluated against that one read: the resources the checks test (VMs, scale sets, disks, snapshots, storage, SQL, App Service, Key Vault, AKS, load balancers, Application Gateways, public IPs, NSGs, NICs, Cosmos DB, Redis, container registries, Recovery Services vaults, virtual networks, resource groups), VM extensions, autoscale settings, deployment slots, what Azure Backup protects, how many alert rules and action groups each subscription has, Azure Advisor's recommendations in the pillars' categories, and Defender for Cloud's plans, secure scores and high-severity assessments.
Each pillar is scored against its design principles (Microsoft Learn): Reliability business requirements, resilience, recovery, operations, simplicity - zones, backups, redundancy, instance counts, retired Basic SKUs, health probes, SLA tiers Security security readiness, confidentiality, integrity, availability, sustained posture - Defender plans and secure score, TLS, HTTPS, public access, network restrictions, keys and local accounts, management ports open to the internet, WAF, DDoS Cost cost-management discipline, cost-efficiency, usage and rate optimization, monitoring - cost-allocation tags (-CostTag), unattached disks, unused public IPs, VMs stopped but billed, empty plans, old snapshots, Azure Hybrid Benefit, old VM generations Operational DevOps culture, standards, observability, deployment, Excellence automation - owner and environment tags (-OwnerTag), the Azure Monitor agent, boot diagnostics, Application Insights, alert rules and action groups, deployment slots, platform patching, AKS auto-upgrade Performance targets, capacity, sustained performance, optimization Efficiency - autoscale on plans, scale sets, AKS and Application Gateway, accelerated networking, SSD OS disks, SQL and Redis tiers Advisor and Defender are checks too, one per pillar (AD-HA, AD-SEC, AD-COST, AD-OPS, AD-PERF, DF-HIGH): a resource with an open recommendation fails. maml:description.maml:para: Lets an enterprise application or managed identity manage specific Entra groups only - not every group in the tenant - with an administrative unit, a custom (or built-in) directory role and a role assignment scoped to the unit. Plan, confirm, apply, verify.

Microsoft Graph application permissions are tenant-wide: GroupMember.ReadWrite.All lets an application add and remove members in every group, and there is no "selected groups" version of it (as Sites.Selected is for SharePoint). The same rights, over chosen groups only: 1. Administrative unit holds exactly the groups (-AdministrativeUnitName; created when missing, -RestrictedManagement on creation) 2. Directory role only the group actions (-Access, or your own -AllowedResourceAction); a custom role (-RoleName) is created, or updated when its actions differ; a built-in role is used as it is 3. Role assignment the role to the application, scoped to the administrative unit - not '/' The application's code doesn't change: it still asks for a https://graph.microsoft.com/.default token and calls POST /groups/{id}/members/$ref. Any other group answers 403.
Like Deploy-AACStorageAccount, it plans first - what exists is read and only what is missing is written - and shows the plan. Findings say what would undo the scope: a tenant-wide Graph permission (GroupMember.ReadWrite.All, Group.ReadWrite.All, Directory.ReadWrite.All - removed with -RemoveTenantWidePermission), the same role at tenant scope, other objects in the unit, dynamic or role-assignable groups. You are asked before anything is written (-Force, or -Confirm:$false, for pipelines); -WhatIf stops after the plan. After the apply everything is read again: running the same command again plans no changes.
Needs the Connect-AAC sign-in with Privileged Role Administrator (or Global Administrator) - a service principal needs the Graph permissions RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory, AdministrativeUnit.ReadWrite.All, Application.Read.All and Group.Read.All, and AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All for -RemoveTenantWidePermission. Custom roles and administrative units need Microsoft Entra ID P1. An application may cache its token for up to an hour (a managed identity up to 24 hours) before the change takes effect.

What the application may do in the groups: MemberReadWrite read the groups and their members, add and remove members (default - the same rights as GroupMember.ReadWrite.All) MemberRead read the groups and their members MemberAndOwnerReadWrite members and owners

Cost Management allows only a few queries a minute, so a progress display shows each subscription as it is read, and throttled requests are retried.
Exports: -CsvPath the detail: one row per subscription, month, resource group and service - SubscriptionName, SubscriptionId, Month, ResourceGroup, Service, Cost, Currency - ready for an Excel pivot table -PdfPath a landscape A4 report: a summary (totals, the subscription-by-month table, top services and resource groups this month), then a page per subscription with its services and resource groups month by month -HtmlPath a self-contained, interactive HTML report: tiles and charts (by month, subscription, service, resource group) that filter the detail, a subscription-by-month table and every detail row, with search, filters, grouping, totals of what is shown and a CSV download -PassThru one AAC.SubscriptionCost object per subscription: MonthToDate, one property per month ('2026-07', ...), Total, TopServices and Status ('OK', 'No cost', or why the subscription couldn't be read)
